cita: Yang, D. (2026). Control-Plane Placement Shapes Forgetting: An Architectural Study of Agent Memory Across Thirteen System Configurations.
problema: Production memory failures are predominantly FORGETTING failures (rotated credentials still recommended, GDPR-deleted records still surfacing) rather than recall failures, yet every existing memory benchmark scores only recall; the control plane (supersede/release/purge) is largely untested, and it is unknown WHERE in the pipeline an LLM should sit to recover which forgetting failure modes.
mecanismo: ForgetEval decomposes forgetting into 5 structural families (supersession, decay, amnesia, purge, drift), scored by deterministic substring match (no LLM judge in the eval loop) across a 1000-case template suite plus a 385-case adversarial layer (10 attack categories: prefix_collision, cross_lingual_identifier, compound_fact, etc.); a 6-method Adapter Protocol (3 mandatory recall primitives + 3 optional mutation primitives with honest N/A scoring) lets heterogeneous memory stores be compared apples-to-apples; compares 13 system configurations spanning 6 placement regimes for WHERE the LLM sits (no-deletion/deterministic/vec-only/inscribe-time-LLM/KG-abstraction/mutation-time-hook).
evaluacion: 13 system configurations (Lethe, Mem0, LangGraph/LangMem, MemPalace + LLM-hook and inscribe-time variants) on the 385-case adversarial suite + 1000-case template suite; cross-evaluation on the Memora benchmark (150 questions/10 personas) to test axis-complementarity; 10-annotator IAA + cross-family LLM-judge audit + 77-case external-authored replication subset; embedder-swap ablation.
numeros_clave: Deterministic systems cluster 62.9-68.3% overall on the 385-case suite; a mutation-time LLM hook lifts non-primitive-existence cases (n=345) by +22.6 to +24.1pt (70.1-70.7% -> 93.3-94.2%), headline overall 91.7-93.2%, at ~$0.17/385-case run, mutation latency ~2.3s/case vs 64-191ms/case deterministic. MemPalace: 0/385 on ForgetEval-Adv (no deletion primitive) but 60/150 (40%) on Memora recall-heavy benchmark (axis-flip).

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: Central claim is that 'production failures are predominantly forgetting failures... yet existing memory benchmarks measure only recall', directly challenging any MF assumption that a well-measured retrieval/recall layer is sufficient; forgetting/deletion is shown to be an independent, under-tested axis (MemPalace: 0/385 forgetting despite 60/150 recall).

The paper's core architectural finding is WHERE the LLM sits relative to the recall vs control (mutation) plane determines which forgetting failure modes recover (S1, Fig.2): inscribe-time LLM fixes canonicalization but not intent-aware deletion, mutation-time hook fixes both -- a concrete placement lesson for where MF should put its own write/forget-trigger LLM calls.

The mutation-time-hook lift (91.7-93.2% overall) costs only ~$0.17/385-case run and ~2.3s/case (mutations only) while leaving the recall hot path LLM-free and unchanged, confirming MF's stance that a targeted, narrowly-scoped LLM call (not a blanket one) can buy large capability gains cheaply.

The five forgetting families (supersession/decay/amnesia/purge/drift) and identifier-canonicalization attacks (cross-script, prefix-collision) are exactly staleness/provenance failure modes MF's FIDELIDAD concern targets, empirically shown recoverable only by specific architectural placements, not by recall quality.

notes: Table 2 385-case adversarial results + Table 3 Memora axis-flip cross-eval + Fig.2 placement regimes, arXiv 2606.15903 v2.

cita: Ma et al. (2026). MEMPROBE: Probing Long-Term Agent Memory via Hidden User-State Recovery.
problema: Memory evaluation relies on downstream task success, which is a weak diagnostic: a memoryless agent achieves near-perfect task success, so task completion cannot distinguish good memory formation from none, and the memory ARTIFACT itself (what durable user state got written and remains recoverable) is left unaudited.
mecanismo: MemProbe treats memory as a post-interaction auditable artifact: 50 simulated users each carry a hidden 31-dimension taxonomy-anchored user-state bank (skill/knowledge/episodic/self-model/assistance-preference); leak-controlled tasks (indirect design + anti-fishing critic) elicit evidence without naming the target; after the trajectory, each hidden dimension is reconstructed from the memory store under two read modes -- full-store dump_all (probes whether evidence was ever WRITTEN) vs top-k retrieve (probes whether it is REACHABLE) -- scored by an LLM judge against ground truth (category-balanced recovery score B); a 3-stage failure-attribution pipeline (task-design / disclosure / elicitation-vs-strictness) localizes where recovery loss occurred.
evaluacion: 5 memory systems (nomem, longctx_full, amem/A-Mem, mem0/Mem0, memt/Mem-T) across 50 simulated users x 31 dimensions (1,550 recovery targets), measuring task-completion rate, preference score, turns, reconstruction score B (full-store vs top-k), and memory footprint.
numeros_clave: All systems saturate task completion at 99.87-99.94% INCLUDING nomem (no memory at all); reconstruction B stays moderate: full-store 0.611-0.624 for amem/mem0/longctx_full vs 0.000 for nomem, dropping to 0.465-0.540 under top-k retrieval. Episodic-memory category is hardest across all systems (0.242-0.451 full-store/top-k) vs assistance-preference easiest (0.721-0.773).

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: The headline finding is that task success and memory formation are DISTINCT capabilities -- a memoryless agent (nomem) attains near-perfect task success (99.935%) yet 0.000 reconstruction, directly challenging any MF assumption that downstream task/behavioral success is a valid proxy for whether durable memory was actually formed.

The dual full-store-vs-top-k read protocol (S3.1) is precisely a measured decomposition of write-side vs read-side failure, confirming MF's stance that retrieval must be measured SEPARATELY from whether information was ever captured, not conflated into one aggregate score.

The paper identifies 'retrieval-aware consolidation' as the major bottleneck: systems capture raw interaction but 'seldom distill it into compact user state' (S1) -- capacity and retrieval tuning alone cannot fix what only a better WRITE/consolidation policy can, challenging any MF assumption that a good retriever compensates for a weak consolidation step.

Table3 shows EPISODIC memory (binding an event to its context and consequence) is the hardest category to recover across every system (0.242-0.451) versus stable preferences (0.721-0.773), confirming MF's fidelity concern that different memory TYPES have measurably different durability and cannot be treated as a single undifferentiated store.

notes: Table 2 main results + Table 3 category breakdown + S3.5 failure-attribution pipeline, arXiv 2606.24595 (preprint, UIC/KU Leuven/UCSD).

cita: Wang (2026). MemDelta: Controlled Baselines and Hidden Confounds in Agent Memory Evaluation.
problema: Agent memory system evaluations conflate the memory ARCHITECTURE with confounded changes in the language model, embedding model, or retrieval pipeline, so it is unclear what a reported 'memory gain' is actually measuring.
mecanismo: MemDelta is a controlled protocol that varies exactly one component at a time (retrieval quality, embedding choice, base-model behavior, write-path cost) while holding the rest of the pipeline fixed (7 strategies: no-memory, random-RAG, full-context, self-memory scratchpad, MiniLM-RAG, cloud-embedding-RAG, Mem0 extraction, on LongMemEval-S), with paired McNemar significance tests and explicit write-path cost accounting (LLM calls, wall-clock, dollars) per strategy.
evaluacion: LongMemEval-S (500 questions, 6 types, 3 model families: GPT-4o-mini/Claude Sonnet/Gemini 2.5 Flash); 6 controlled pairwise comparisons isolating each confound; matched-instance cost-accuracy audit of Mem0 vs verbatim RAG on 88 instances.
numeros_clave: Verbatim RAG (MiniLM) matches full-context GPT-4o-mini (47.2% vs 49.8%, p=0.34), but the ranking reverses per model: Sonnet gains +31pp from RAG (63% of full-context queries refused) while Gemini gains +14pp from full context. A single embedding swap (MiniLM->cloud) shifts accuracy +6.2pp (p=0.004) and flips Mem0-vs-RAG: Mem0 beats MiniLM-RAG by +11pp but loses to cloud-RAG by -1.2pp. On 88 matched instances, Mem0 (72.7%) ties cloud RAG (73.9%, p=1.0) at 50x the write-path cost.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: The paper's core demonstration is that a reported '+11pp memory architecture gain' (Mem0 vs RAG) was ENTIRELY an embedding confound that reverses to -1.2pp under a single component swap, directly challenging any MF claim attributing an observed gain to a memory-architecture decision without holding embeddings/model/cost fixed.

The matched-instance audit shows Mem0 ties verbatim RAG (72.7% vs 73.9%) at 50x the write-path cost (1,000+ LLM calls, $0.50+, ~120min vs $0.01/instance), confirming MF's stance that write-path cost must be reported alongside accuracy before crediting an architecture with a gain.

The recommended protocol (report a named-embedding RAG baseline, include random retrieval, test >=2 model families, disclose embedding-swap sensitivity, report write-path cost) is a direct, actionable methodology for how MF should measure its own retrieval layer to avoid confounded conclusions.

The Sonnet case study (63% of full-context queries explicitly refused despite the answer being present in the 115K-token context, dropping to 41% at 47K tokens) shows apparent 'memory failure' can actually be a model-specific long-context attention failure unrelated to the memory system, confirming MF should separate storage/retrieval fidelity from generator behavior when diagnosing failures.

notes: Table 3 main results + Table 5 embedding ablation + Table 6/7 matched cost-accuracy audit, arXiv 2606.29914.

cita: Filatov (2026). RPR-Memory: Decomposing Retrieval, Policy, and Reasoning in Persistent Memory Systems.
problema: Persistent-memory benchmarks reduce evaluation to one aggregate score, hiding WHERE a system fails: missing evidence (retrieval), wrong exposed state (read-time policy), or failed composition (reasoning), so an apparent 'memory failure' cannot be localized or fixed.
mecanismo: RPR-Memory decomposes persistent-memory pipelines into three diagnostic layers (Retrieval R+, read-time Policy, Reasoning A+) via a per-(system,query) 2x2 matrix (R+A+/R+A-/R-A+/R-A-) and three hard probes (compositional-chain, version/supersession, temporal-window) run through a common six-primitive interface (write/read/search/update/forget/consolidate) wrapping 37 heterogeneous architectures; a controlled 3-arm causal intervention (original / write-time-supersession-only / read-time query-conditioned router) on one in-house semantic-fact store isolates whether a 'memory failure' is fixable at write time or read time.
evaluacion: 37 memory architectures (35 in-house + Mem0 v2.0.2 + HippoRAG v2.0.0a4) on 3 hard probes (chain n=50/51q, version n=50/152q, temporal n=50/150q) under a fixed local llama3.1:8b composer; a post-freeze temporal ladder + 6-participant human pilot comparing strict vs semantic EM; external-only sensitivity check; controlled write/read-time intervention with pre-registered falsification bound.
numeros_clave: Retrieval saturates before correctness: chain R+=0.977 but P(A+|R+)=0.377; temporal R+=0.968 but P=0.314 (between-window subtype collapses to P=0.027 despite R+=0.987). Version-resolution causal core: adding write-time supersession lifts current-state update correctness from 0.000 to 0.680 but breaks history-sensitive exact match (0.816->0.355); only a query-conditioned read-time router recovers both. Human pilot: between-window rows move from 0.000 strict to 0.967 semantic EM, while the model stays at 0.078 even with oracle-filtered candidates.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: The paper's central methodology, a per-axis R+/P(A+|R+) matrix that separates retrieval success from post-retrieval correctness (Table3/Fig.2), is exactly the measured, decomposed retrieval evaluation MF's G-M2 need calls for, showing retrieval can saturate (R+=0.977) while conditional correctness stays low (0.377), which an aggregate score would hide.

The version-resolution finding that 'read-time state exposure is a separate, repairable layer' distinct from write-time supersession gives MF a concrete architectural distinction between what to STOP writing (superseded facts) vs what to FILTER at read time, informing a negative-knowledge/staleness design that need not conflate the two.

The causal intervention shows write-time supersession ALONE creates a seam conflict: fixing current-state correctness (0.000->0.680) actively BREAKS history-sensitive exact match (0.816->0.355) in the same store, challenging any MF assumption that a single write-time policy can serve both current-state and historical-lookup needs without a read-time query-conditioned split.

The paper shows a system can achieve high aggregate exact match (0.816) while stale-hit leakage is 1.000 and current-state update correctness is 0.000 (the 'motivating paradox'), directly confirming MF's fidelity/staleness concern that aggregate accuracy can mask complete failure on the specific state-resolution behavior a query needs.

notes: Table 3/4/5 retrieval-vs-correctness decomposition + Table 8 human-pilot temporal ladder, arXiv preprint 2026-07-01, independent researcher.

cita: Xiang et al. (2026). MemSyco-Bench: Benchmarking Sycophancy in Agent Memory.
problema: Existing memory benchmarks evaluate only whether memories are correctly stored, retrieved, or updated, ignoring how retrieved memories influence downstream reasoning; this overlooks 'memory-induced sycophancy', where agents over-align with outdated or inapplicable historical user beliefs at the cost of factual accuracy or objective reasoning.
mecanismo: MemSyco-Bench defines 5 task categories: 3 where memory should be SUPPRESSED (Objective Fact Judgment, Contextual Scope Control, Memory-Evidence Conflict) and 2 where memory should be SELECTED/USED correctly (Valid Memory Selection, Personalized Memory Use), built via a 4-step pipeline: memory-decision schema construction, question instantiation with target vs memory-misleading answers, long-term dialogue simulation embedding memory cues naturally, and multi-stage quality validation (semantic relatedness, memory-use boundary, failure direction).
evaluacion: Preliminary studies establish that memory snippets induce sycophancy and that existing benchmarks' errors are retrieval-driven; main experiments evaluate 7 memory systems (NaiveRAG, Mem0, A-Mem, LightMem, MemGPT, MemoryBank, SuperMemory) x 2 backbones (Qwen3-8B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash) across the 5 tasks, reporting Accuracy plus Sycophancy Rate / Memory-Use Metrics.
numeros_clave: Preliminary: adding a misleading memory snippet drops DeepSeek-V4-Flash's objective accuracy from 56.1% to 40.2% and raises sycophancy rate from 24.3% to 52.3%. Existing benchmarks are retrieval-dominated: R-/A- accounts for 47.4-66.1% of errors vs R+/A- only 5.8-13.7% (Fig.3). Main results (Qwen3-8B, Objective Fact Judgment): No-Memory 49.12% Acc vs memory-system settings 26.00-36.00% (all WORSE); Contextual Scope Control sycophancy rate for Mem0/LightMem hits 51.00/79.67% vs Full-Dialog baseline 40.33%.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: Existing memory benchmarks' errors are dominated by retrieval failure (R-/A- = 47.4-66.1%) while post-retrieval misuse (R+/A-) is rare (5.8-13.7%) in THOSE benchmarks, yet on MemSyco-Bench's own tasks memory systems actively WORSEN accuracy vs a no-memory baseline, challenging any MF assumption that solving retrieval is sufficient once post-retrieval reasoning is also measured.

Central finding is that current memory systems (Mem0, A-Mem, LightMem, MemGPT, etc.) 'do not reliably mitigate memory-induced sycophancy' and often move sycophancy rate in the WRONG direction relative to a no-memory/full-dialog baseline (Table1), directly challenging any MF assumption that adding a memory layer is safe by default without an explicit mechanism to suppress inapplicable retrieved memory.

The five-task taxonomy cleanly separates 'memory should be suppressed' (objective facts, scope, evidence-conflict) from 'memory should be selected/used' (valid-selection, personalization) as DISTINCT decision problems (S3.2), a seam MF's own retrieval/generation-gating policy could adopt to decide per-query whether a retrieved memory should influence the answer at all.

The R+/A+ vs R+/A- vs R-/A- error-attribution protocol (S2.2, Fig.3) used to show existing benchmarks are retrieval-dominated is itself a measured decomposition of retrieval success from generation-time correctness, confirming MF's stance that retrieval and post-retrieval use must be measured as separate axes.

notes: Fig.2/3 preliminary studies + Table 1 main results (5 tasks x 7 memory systems x 2 backbones), arXiv 2607.01071 v2, work-in-progress (Xiamen/Jilin).

cita: Roth et al. (2024). Pairing Analogy-Augmented Generation with Procedural Memory for Procedural Q&A.
problema: LLMs struggle to synthesize disparate pieces of information into a coherent procedure for unfamiliar/specialized domains (not well-represented in training data); plain RAG retrieves generic text passages rather than adapting analogous prior PROCEDURES (input/output/ordered-steps) via structural/relational similarity to a new task.
mecanismo: Analogy-Augmented Generation (AAG): a procedural memory store holds procedures (input, output, ordered steps) as dense 768-d embeddings (all-mpnet-base-v2), written once and retrieved by cosine similarity; a query generator decomposes the input query into up to N=4 HyDE-style sub-questions to retrieve K=3 analogous procedures per sub-question; an answer generator filters/synthesizes each retrieved analogy into a Q&A context; an iterative LLM-critic self-refinement loop (up to T=3 cycles) edits the draft procedure until no further edits are suggested.
evaluacion: LLM-based pairwise evaluation (10 calls/sample, position-debiased, majority vote) vs Zero-Shot/Few-Shot/RAG/ReAct baselines on LCStep (unfamiliar domain, 276 LangChain-tutorial procedures) and RecipeNLG (familiar domain, 10k-recipe subset); corroborated by a blind human study on RecipeNLG (50 examples, 3-6 raters/pair); full ablation removing each of the 3 AAG components (query generator, answer generator, critic refinement) in all permutations; also surveyed on CHAMP (math) in the appendix.
numeros_clave: Table1 pairwise vs RAG: AAG wins 69.64% / loses 12.50% (LCStep); wins 85.70% / loses 7.60% (RecipeNLG). Vs ReAct: AAG wins 98.21% (LCStep) / 97.65% (RecipeNLG). Blind human study on RecipeNLG (50 examples): AAG preferred in 56% of instances vs RAG preferred in 16% (28% tie). Ablation vs NO-answer-generator: AAG wins only 39.28%/loses 39.28% on LCStep (near-tie, component matters less there) but wins 58.45%/loses 26.20% on RecipeNLG (component matters clearly there).

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: Procedural memory stores structured (input,output,steps) objects retrieved by embedding similarity and then ADAPTED via analogy rather than copied verbatim (S4.1-4.3); the composability property (two procedures chain into one) lets stored steps be recombined, a derived-index pattern MF could adopt for procedural playbooks distinct from factual retrieval.

The full ablation (Table1, removing query-generator/answer-generator/critic in all permutations, scored by pairwise LLM judging) isolates each pipeline component's marginal contribution rather than reporting only end-to-end task success, confirming MF's stance that a retrieval/analogy mechanism's value must be measured component-by-component -- and the ablation shows the answer-generator's contribution is domain-dependent (near-tie on LCStep, clear on RecipeNLG), not uniformly load-bearing.

notes: Table 1 pairwise win/loss/tie (LCStep + RecipeNLG) + S5.5 human study (56% vs 16%) + S5.6 ablation permutations, arXiv 2409.01344 (2024, EMNLP-era; older cohort than the corpus's typical 2026 papers but on-topic for procedural memory).
